source_text: Καὶ τί μοι τὸ λοιπὸν τὸ πλῆθος τῶν τοιούτων ὀνομασιῶν καὶ γενεαλογιῶν καταλέγειν; Ὥστε κατὰ πάντα τρόπον ἐμπαίζονται οἱ συγγραφεῖς πάντες καὶ ποιηταὶ καὶ φιλόσοφοι λεγόμενοι, ἔτι μὴν καὶ οἱ προσέχοντες αὐτοῖς, Μύθους γὰρ μᾶλλον καὶ μωρίας συνέταξαν περὶ τῶν κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς θεῶν· οὐ γὰρ ἀπέδειξαν αὐτοὺς θεοὺς ἀλλὰ ἀνθρώπους, οὓς μὲν μεθύσους, ἑτέρους πόρνους καὶ φονεῖς. Ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τῆς κοσμογονίας ἀσύμφωνα ἀλλήλοις καὶ φαῦλα ἐξεῖπον. Πρῶτον μὲν ὅτι τινὲς ἀγένητον τὸν κόσμον ἀπεφήναντο, καθὼς καὶ ἔμπροσθεν ἐδηλώσαμεν. Καὶ οἱ μὲν ἀγένητον αὐτὸν καὶ ἀΐδιον φύσιν φάσκοντες οὐκ ἀκόλουθα εἶπον τοῖς γενητὸν αὐτὸν δογματίσασιν. Εἰκασμῷ γὰρ ταῦτα καὶ ἀνθρωπίνῃ ἐννοίᾳ ἐφθέγξαντο, καὶ οὐ κατὰ ἀλήθειαν. Ἕτεροι δ᾿ αὖ εἶπον πρόνοιαν εἶναι, καὶ τὰ τούτων δόγματα ἀνέλυσαν. Ἄρατος μὲν οὖν φησιν· Ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεσθα, τὸν οὐδέποτ᾿ ἄνδρες ἐῶμεν Ἄῤῥητον· μεσταὶ δὲ Διὸς πᾶσαι μὲν ἀγυιαί, Πᾶσαι δ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἀγοραί, μεστὴ δὲ θάλασσα Καὶ λιμένες· πάντη δὲ Διὸς κεχρήμεθα πάντες. Τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν· ὁ δ᾿ ἤπιος ἀνθρώποισιν Δεξιὰ σημαίνει, λαοὺς δ᾿ ἐπὶ ἔργον ἐγείρει Μιμνήσκων βιότοιο· λέγει δ᾿ ὅτε βῶλος ἀρίστη Βουσί τε καὶ μακέλῃσι, λέγει δ᾿ ὅτε δεξιαὶ ὧραι Καὶ φυτὰ γυρῶσαι καὶ σπέρματα πάντα βαλέσθαι. Τίνι οὖν πιστεύσωμεν, πότερον Ἀράτῳ ἢ Σοφοκλεῖ λέγοντι Πρόνοια δ᾿ ἐστὶν οὐδενὸς [σαφής], Εἰκῆ κράτιστον ζῆν ὅπως δύναιτό τις; Ὅμηρος δὲ πάλιν τούτῳ οὐ συνᾴδει. Λέγει γάρ· Ζεὺς δ᾿ ἀρετὴν ἄνδρεσσιν ὀφέλλει τε μινύθει τε. Καὶ Σιμωνίδης· Οὔτις ἄνευ θεῶν Ἀρετὰν λάβεν, οὐ πόλις, οὐ βροτός. Θεὸς ὁ παμμῆτις· ἀπήμαντον δ᾿ οὐδὲν Ἔστιν ἐν αὐτοῖς. Ὁμοίως καὶ Εὐριπίδης· Οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδὲν χωρὶς ἀνθρώποις θεοῦ. Καὶ Μένανδρος· Οὐκ ἄρα φροντίζει τις ἡμῶν ἢ μόνος θεός. Καὶ πάλιν Εὐριπίδης· Σῶσαι γὰρ ὁπόταν τῷ θεῷ δοκῇ, Πολλὰς προφάσεις δίδωσιν εἰς σωτηρίαν. Καὶ [Θέστιος]· Θεοῦ θέλοντος σώζῃ, κἂν ἐπὶ ῥιπὸς πλέῃς. Καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα μυρία εἰπόντες ἀσύμφωνα ἑαυτοῖς ἐξεῖπον. Ὁ γοῦν Σοφοκλῆς ἀπρονοησίαν ἐν ἑτέρῳ λέγων· Θεοῦ δὲ πληγὴν οὐχ ὑπερπηδᾷ βροτός. Πλὴν καὶ πληθὺν εἰσήγαγον ἢ καὶ μοναρχίαν εἷπον, καὶ πρόνοιαν εἶναι τοῖς λέγουσιν ἀπρονοησίαν τἀναντία εἰρήκασιν. Ὁθεν Εὐριπίδης ὁμολογεῖ λέγων· Σπουδάζομεν δὲ πολλ᾿ ὑπ᾿ ἐλπίδων, μάτην Πόνους ἔχοντες, οὐδὲν εἰδότες. Καὶ μὴ θέλοντες ὁμολογοῦσιν τὸ ἀληθὲς μὴ ἐπίστασθαι· ὑπὸ δαιμόνων δὲ ἐμπνευσθέντες καὶ ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν φυσιωθέντες ἃ εἶπον δι᾿ αὐτῶν εἶπον. Ἤτοι γὰρ οἱ ποιηταί, Ὅμηρος δὴ καὶ Ἡσίοδος, ὥς φασιν ὑπὸ Μουσῶν ἐμπνευσθέντες, φαντασίᾳ καὶ πλάνῃ ἐλάλησαν, καὶ οὐ καθαρῷ πνεύματι ἀλλὰ πλάνῳ. Ἐκ τούτου δὲ σαφῶς δείκνυται, εἰ καὶ οἱ δαιμονῶντες ἐνίοτε καὶ μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο ἐξορκίζονται κατὰ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ ὄντως θεοῦ, καὶ ὁμολογεῖ αὐτὰ τὰ πλάνα πνεύματα εἶναι δαίμονες, οἱ καὶ τότε εἰς ἐκείνους ἐνεργήσαντες· πλὴν ἐνίοτέ τινες τῇ ψυχῇ ἐκνήψαντες ἐξ αὐτῶν εἶπον ἀκόλουθα τοῖς προφήταις, ὅπως εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς τε καὶ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις, περί τε θεοῦ μοναρχίας καὶ κρίσεως καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ὧν ἔφασαν.
pass_a_gloss: What need is there for me to recount the multitude of such names and genealogies? So in every way, all writers and poets and philosophers, and even those who pay attention to them, are deceived. For they have composed myths and foolishness about the gods they speak of, not demonstrating them to be gods, but rather humans, some of whom are drunkards, others are fornicators and murderers. But they have also spoken discordant and vile things about the creation of the world. First, some have declared the world to be uncreated, as we previously showed. And those who say it is uncreated and eternal in nature have not spoken consistently with those who claim it is created. For they have spoken these things by conjecture and human thought, and not according to truth. Others, on the other hand, have said that providence exists, and they have analyzed their own doctrines. Aratus, for example, says: 'We begin with Zeus, whom men never leave unspoken.' And all the streets and marketplaces of men are full of Zeus, and the sea and harbors are full of him; and we all have need of him, for we are his offspring. And he is gentle to men, showing his right hand, and rousing the people to work, reminding them of their livelihood. He speaks when the soil is best for plowing and for sowing all seeds. So whom should we believe, Aratus or Sophocles, who says: 'There is no clear providence; it is best to live as one can'? But Homer does not agree with this. For he says: 'Zeus gives virtue to men and increases it.' And Simonides: 'No one obtains virtue without the gods, neither city nor mortal.' God is all-wise; nothing is without him. Similarly, Euripides: 'There is nothing without God for men.' And Menander: 'No one cares for us except God alone.' And again Euripides: 'For when it seems good to God, he saves, giving many pretexts for salvation.' And Thesius: 'If God wills, you will be saved, even if you sail on a raft.' And having said such things, they have spoken discordantly with themselves. For Sophocles, speaking of the neglect of God, says: 'No mortal can escape the blow of God.' Moreover, they have introduced a multitude or even a monarchy, and those who say providence exists have said the opposite, neglect. Therefore, Euripides confesses, saying: 'We strive for many things in vain, having troubles, knowing nothing.' And unwillingly, they confess that they do not know the truth; for they have been inspired by demons and have been possessed by them, and they have spoken what they said through them. For the poets, Homer and Hesiod, as they say, having been inspired by the Muses, spoke with fantasy and error, and not with a pure spirit, but with error. From this, it is clearly shown that even those who are possessed by demons are sometimes exorcised in the name of the true God, and the spirits of error confess that they are demons, who were at work in those people at that time. However, at times some people, having awakened in their soul, have spoken consistently with the prophets, so that they might be a testimony to them and to all people, concerning the monarchy of God and judgment and the other things they said.
pass_b_english: Why should I go on listing the countless names and genealogies of such figures? In every respect the writers, poets, and philosophers — and even those who follow them — are deceived. They have fabricated myths and sheer foolishness about the gods they describe, failing to prove those beings are divine; instead they portray them as mere humans, some drunkards, others fornicators and murderers.

They also speak discordantly and vilely about the origin of the world. First, some declared the world uncreated, as we have already shown. Those who claim it is uncreated and eternal by nature do not speak consistently with those who assert it was created; they rely on conjecture and human reasoning, not on truth. Others, on the other hand, maintain that providence exists and then analyze their own teachings. Aratus, for instance, says: “We begin with Zeus, whom men never leave unspoken; all streets, marketplaces, seas, and harbors are full of him, and we all need him, for we are his offspring. He is gentle to humanity, extending his right hand, rousing people to work and reminding them of their livelihood, telling when the soil is best for plowing and for sowing every seed.” So whom should we trust — Aratus or Sophocles, who declares, “There is no clear providence; it is best to live as one can”? Homer disagrees, saying, “Zeus gives virtue to men and increases it.” Simonides adds, “No one obtains virtue without the gods, neither city nor mortal.” God is all‑wise; nothing exists apart from him. Euripides echoes, “There is nothing without God for men.” Menander states, “No one cares for us except God alone.” Euripides again: “When it seems good to God, he saves, providing many pretexts for salvation.” And Thesius: “If God wills, you will be saved, even if you sail on a raft.” Yet having said all this, they contradict themselves. Sophocles, speaking of divine neglect, says, “No mortal can escape the blow of God.” Moreover they have introduced a multitude of deities or even a single monarchy, and those who affirm providence have simultaneously asserted its opposite, neglect. Consequently Euripides confesses, “We strive for many things in vain, enduring troubles while knowing nothing.” Reluctantly they admit they do not know the truth, for they have been inspired and possessed by demons, and they spoke through those spirits.

The poets Homer and Hesiod, as they claim, were inspired by the Muses, yet they spoke in fantasy and error, not by a pure spirit but by deception. From this it is clearly shown that even those who are possessed by demons are sometimes exorcised in the name of the true God, and the errant spirits themselves confess they are demons who were active in those individuals at that time. Nevertheless, at times certain people, awakened in their souls, have spoken in agreement with the prophets, so that they may serve as a testimony to the prophets and to all humanity concerning the monarchy of God, his judgment, and the other matters the prophets declared.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the complex arguments regarding the nature of the world (uncreated vs. created) and the various conflicting views on providence expressed by the cited poets. All quotes from Aratus, Sophocles, Homer, Simonides, Euripides, Menander, and Thesius are faithfully rendered in both Pass A and B. The distinction between being inspired by Muses/demons versus a pure spirit is preserved. No omissions or additions were noted.
